In brief

The chapters of Ulysses have no numbers (this website adds them in square brackets) or titles, but Joyce supplied virtual titles in two strange charts that he shared with confidants near the time of the novel's publication, associating each chapter with a certain "episode" in Homer's Odyssey. Headnotes like this one ask how the chapters recast their Homeric originals and how the 18-chapter structure of the novel reflects the 24-book structure of the epic poem. They also identify each chapter's geographical location and time of day, and many of them discuss narrative techniques. Episode 1, "Telemachus" according to the schemas, echoes the situation found in the palace on Ithaca at the beginning of the ancient epic. Most of the action takes place in a decommissioned military tower on the rocky coast of Sandycove, seven miles southeast of central Dublin, with a short walk to a nearby swimming hole at the end of the chapter. Things begins a little after 8 AM on 16 June 1904 and conclude at 8:45.

At more length

If Joyce had not titled his work Ulysses or suggested links to the Odyssey in his schemas, readers might have wandered in the dark for decades before suspecting such a design. Even today many people are inclined to dismiss the Homeric correspondences as pretentious claptrap, some suspecting that Joyce's interest never advanced beyond his childhood encounter with Charles Lamb's The Adventures of Ulysses. I suspect that many of these skeptics are themselves not reading the Odyssey. Joyce dreamed up additional kinds of structure as he went along—deploying newspaper-like headlines in Aeolus, say, or imitating Catholic catechisms in Ithaca—but his interest in Homer only deepened. Ulysses is engaged in a multifarious, though neither comprehensive nor straightforward, intertextual dialogue with the Odyssey. The novel evokes the epic poem opportunistically, in ways that vary dramatically from chapter to chapter. The echoes are quirky, unsystematic, imaginative, and often hilarious, but they also provoke thought about the commonalities in ancient and modern human life. Sometimes they are so exceedingly subtle that a century's worth of readings have failed to appreciate their extensiveness—a deficit that I hope to remedy to some extent.

The first three chapters of Ulysses are preceded by a Roman numeral I, signifying that they constitute a distinct section. A Roman II introduces chapters 4-15, while chapters 16-18 constitute section III. The first four books of Homer's poem, often called the Telemacheia or Telemachiad, show a young man (20 years old) struggling to believe that his father could still be alive and determined to reclaim his throne. Joyce's first three chapters similarly belong to a young man (age 22) struggling to grow into adult confidence and agency, and thinking about spiritual paternity. Chapter 4 of Ulysses, like book 5 of the Odyssey, introduces an older man who is destined eventually to unite with the younger one, but the order of events in this section of the novel is very different from Homer's, as I detail in the headnote to this chapter. The final section of Ulysses returns to a fairly close imitation of the order of events in the Odyssey, though it compacts the action from 12 books to 3 chapters.

Joyce's first novel, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, was a bildungsroman (an "education novel" about a young person coming of age) or künstlerroman (the same, but describing the development of an artist), and he continued the story of Stephen Dedalus into Ulysses. But the mature novel shows Stephen far removed from the hopeful sense of purpose that he felt at the end of A Portrait, where he intended to fly by the nets flung at the soul, escape to Paris, and forge the uncreated conscience of his race. In this book Stephen is back in Ireland, immersed again in the misery of his family, living with an Englishman in a tower built by the British empire, tormented by Catholic guilt, overshadowed by a superficially more brilliant and successful companion, hungering for love, drinking too much, and writing only a few impressionistic and derivative lines of verse.

Homer's poem offered a narrative analogue capable of giving structure to the amorphous mass of Stephen's suffering and striving, much as the story of Dedalus and Icarus did in A Portrait. Joyce's Telemachiad, however, is anything but a simple rewriting of Homer's. It is instructive to consider what he did not include, or included only in glancing and ironic ways. Homer's Telemachus is holding down the fort for his father—or wishing that he could. The action is centered on Ithaca, whose palace has been overrun by insolent young men seeking to marry his mother. Joyce does not really map this story onto Stephen's, though he echoes it in many ways.

Mulligan's not paying the rent for the tower, and his determination to drink away the fruits of Stephen's teaching labors, are almost certainly meant to evoke the suitors' riotous consumption of the palace's food and drink. Likewise, Mulligan's contemptuous and contemptible treatment of his aunt's servant (he steals a mirror from her, and jokes about seducing her) recalls the suitors' corruption of the palace's female servants. The old woman who comes to deliver the milk makes Stephen think that she may be a "messenger" or a goddess in disguise, recalling Athena's disguised embassy to Telemachus.

Less obviously, the chapter is stuffed with suggestions of violence. Kinch the knife-blade, Mulligan's razor and surgical lancet, Haines' revolver, a breakfast knife that hews and lunges and impales, references to military barracks and expeditions and defenses, emotional "gaping wounds," thoughts of castration, bodies "cut up into tripes in the dissecting room," ghouls that chew on corpses: all these details recreate the atmosphere of the palace in Ithaca, where 108 young men assault Odysseus' patrimony, threaten the life of his son, and invite the violent destruction that both king and prince rain down upon them at the end of the epic.

But Joyce's first chapter contains no patriarchal homestead, and the allusions suggesting that Stephen might need to protect his wealth, journey in search of his father, and violently defend his home from invaders prove to be red herrings. He may have "paid the rent" on one occasion, but it is clear that he is living in Mulligan's home rather than the other way around, and that Mulligan is supporting him with clothes and money. Violent antipathy may lurk just beneath the surface of the two men's relationship, but Joyce's novel is a deeply pacifist work, and when personal experience gave him material for Stephen to be threatened with bodily injury in the tower, he toned it down. The old milkwoman is no Athena; she does not come to advise Stephen, and he scorns "to beg her favour." The tower lies close to the water, but the hydrophobic Stephen will not be launching a ship; it is Mulligan who plunges into the sea at the chapter's end.

What does survive Joyce's transformations intact is Homer's psychological portrait of a young hero in the making. Mulligan presents himself as Stephen's friend, benefactor, and mentor, but Stephen sees him as a disrespectful, malicious "Usurper" who would, as he says much later in Circe, "Break my spirit." Symbolically, this identifies Mulligan with the chief suitor, Antinous, whose name means "anti-mind." Telemachus's need to assert adult male independence of his mother (he, not she, is the patriarchal heir and presumptive master of the household) takes the form of Stephen's need to overcome the religious guilt associated with his mother's dying. Telemachus's physical search for the father who can help him slaughter his enemies becomes Stephen's need to realize an idea of spiritual paternity that he sees as synonymous with authorship. The book will steer him toward an actual man, Leopold Bloom, who may somehow give Stephen an image of this spiritual ideal, but it will not join the two men in any practical sense comparable to what happens in the Odyssey.

Rather than narrating an existential threat to a kingdom, Joyce's chapter represents a crisis in the psychological development of an individual. Stephen has no Ithaca to restore, but he does need to find a home, both in the literal sense that when he walks away at the end of the chapter he is becoming homeless, and in the larger sense that he needs the familial love and stability that Bloom has found (but is in danger of losing). He needs an artistic purpose, if he is not to reenact the futility of his father's life. He needs a personal strength equal to the forces of British colonial subjection, Catholic puritanical self-denial, Irish political violence, and Dubliners' alcoholic fatalism. These desperate needs of a spectacularly gifted young man make Stephen a Telemachus.

Readers new to the novel will be struck by many stylistic idiosyncrasies. Some are small, like the use of an introductory dash to signal spoken dialogue, rather than quotation marks, and avoidance of hyphens. Others are more consequential, like heavy reliance on "interior monologue" and "free indirect discourse." Joyce's stylistic choices would have marked the book as distinctly avant-garde in 1922, and they still take some getting used to. But it does not take long to make the necessary mental adjustments to what Joyce called his "initial style," and its familiar presence continues throughout the first nine chapters. Chapters 7 and 9 add some dramatic ornaments to this style but do not radically disrupt it. Starting with chapter 10, however, Joyce repeatedly pulls the rug out from under his readers' feet, in an exhilarating series of narrative experiments.

John Hunt 2017
